utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Seselj, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, yes. For the moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Prosecution it's trial attorney Daniel Saxon, and my name is Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I am about to inform you, Mr. Seselj, officially, although I am aware that you have been made aware of this already, that Mr. Aleksandar Lazarevic is no longer standby counsel, not because you requested his removal, but because as a consequence of what you stated during the last Status Conference, he decided to take a criminal action against you for slander, and that created a status of conflict of interest, and he would no longer remain as a standby counsel. So he has now been replaced by a Dutch lawyer, Mr. Tjarda Eduard van der Spoel, as per decision of the Registrar dated the 16th of February, 2004. Mr. van der Spoel is Dutch, as I explained earlier on. He was lead Defence counsel in the case of Jean Kambanda, the former Prime Minister of Rwanda in the proceedings which were conducted before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. He was sworn in as an attorney in Rotterdam way back in 1982 and he specialised in criminal law. He is a member of the Dutch bar association, a member of the board, in fact the treasurer of the Dutch Association of Defence Counsel and chairman of the board and co-founder of the Rotterdam Association of Defence Counsel. Mr. van der Spoel, I suppose, has already been made aware of the terms of reference that this Tribunal set out when Mr. Lazarevic was appointed. If it's not the case, please speak out, Mr. van der Spoel. I want to welcome you on board. You are not and you have not been appointed as Defence counsel for the accused. In fact, the accused has a right to obtain legal advice from a counsel of his own choice, provided this is done in fulfilment of the requirements of our Rules. So once more, welcome. I recognise your presence here in the courtroom. I will proceed with stating for the benefit of the public, in particular, the reasons for this Trial Chamber holding a Status Conference. The last Status Conference was held way back on the 29th of October, 2003. In terms of and pursuant to Rule 65 bis of our Rules, the Trial Chamber is required to hold a Status Conference not later than 120 days after the previous Status Conference, and the purpose of such Status Conferences is to organise exchanges between the parties to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial and to give an opportunity to the accused to raise issues in relation to his or her mental and physical condition, as well as conditions relating to his detention. And I want to start this Status Conference by making a direct reference to a matter that was raised by the accused during the last Status Conference, following which the Trial Chamber indicated that it will be taking direct interest, investigate the matter, and if necessary, hold an additional Status Conference. When we approached the end of the previous Status Conference, Dr. Seselj complained that, with regard to his health condition, he needed surgical intervention and had been ignored, with the result that for three months he had not been given any attention at all and that he complained that this situation could no longer be tolerated and was being detrimental to his health. I did investigate straight away, immediately after the Status Conference, only to find out that, albeit it was true that he needed a surgical intervention, yet he was fully aware, as from a day previous to the Status Conference itself, that an appointment had been made for him for the week after to have this surgical intervention carried out. I have a report from two persons indicating that Dr. Seselj was fully aware that this matter was being attended to and that it would have been resolved the week after. I do want to register my regret that you, Dr. Seselj, took advantage of the situation and instead of complaining that this could have taken a shorter time, you misled the Trial Chamber into believing that this matter was not receiving attention when you were actually aware that it was and that the appointment for surgical intervention had already been fixed and it had been brought to your notice. I hope that in your future dealing with this Trial Chamber, with me in particular, as a Pre-Trial Judge, you will be more honest and not try to mislead me or the Trial Chamber into believing things that are not true. And I send my message right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your interpretation does not correspond to the facts. Are you going to allow me to say what I have to say now? First of all, I waited three months for that surgical intervention, and there is no country in the world wherefore such an operation you have to wait for three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Stop. I will only allow you to explain why you had been told a day before that there was an appointment for your surgical intervention, and instead of giving that information, passing that information to me as the Pre-Trial Judge, you hid that from me. You just complained that you had been waiting for three months, without telling me that you were aware that the intervention was going to take place the week after. If you have an explanation for that, come forward. If you don't, shut up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hide anything from you, and it was to be expected, as in all other cases, that in preparing for a Status Conference, you gather the necessary information as to the health of the accused, who is to appear before you. Secondly, I officially was not informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- about the surgical intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Are you denying that you had been made aware that the surgical intervention was going to be carried out the week after?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am denying that. The nurse told me that it might be the following week, just as she told me that on two or three previous occasions, that it could be in a week's time and wasn't in a week's time. So officially, I was not made aware of that, and it is the head of the Detention Unit who, as a rule, informs the accused about that, and not a nurse, who has no means of influencing the course of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not for you to decide who tells you what. I am informed, and I have no reason to doubt the information that I have been given, that you were formally informed by the nurse and maybe by others, that the surgical intervention was on schedule for the week after, and that closes the matter, as far as I am concerned, and I am advising you not to take this attitude with me, as the Pre-Trial Judge in this case, because I will react. The first matter on the agenda for --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will speak only when I let you speak, Dr. Seselj. The first item on the agenda is issues related to disclosure, and I will first inform you that the Prosecution filed its second report concerning disclosure, which was partly confidential, and in it, the first thing that transpires is that the Prosecution indicates that Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure has not been completed because the Prosecution sought the non-disclosure of some witness statements in the motion of the 10 September 2003 and were awaiting for the Trial Chamber's decision. You can refer this to transcript page 125. The Trial Chamber issued its decision on the 11th February, and in it, it decided two things. First is that the Trial Chamber granted the request for the issuance of a non-disclosure order under Rule 53(A), and secondly, it ordered the Prosecution to provide more information to enable the Trial Chamber to determine the request for pre-trial protective measures. I checked earlier on today whether you have been served with a copy in your own language of this decision by the Trial Chamber. I am informed that you have been served with a copy today, and that is unfortunate, because I precisely made sure that this decision was handed down on the 11th of February, in order to enable you to have it served with it in advance, well in advance of this Status Conference. Unfortunately, it didn't. I'm just advising you that if you feel aggrieved by this decision, you have a right of appeal and rather than discussing it here, you should make use of that right, should you decide to do so. With regard to the second part of that decision, I will come to that later on in another part of today's agenda of this Status Conference. Now, with regard to disclosure relating to Rule 67 material, in the course of the last Status Conference, the accused provided the Prosecution with a document of approximately 80 pages in the Serbo-Croat language, under Rule 67(A)(ii)(b) relating to a special offence. Although the Rule mentions that the Defence shall notify of Prosecutor of its intent to offer a special defence, I had asked to be provided with a courtesy copy, as one can read through the transcript of the last Status Conference. The Prosecution did not object, and I'm grateful for that. And the 80 pages supplied, forwarded by Dr. Seselj have now been translated and a copy of the translated version was handed to me on Monday, the 9th February. I have it here. I have started reading it. I haven't finished as yet. The Prosecution pointed out in its second report concerning disclosure that it too is reviewing Dr. Seselj's document, with a view to determining the factual and legal issues that are in dispute. This determination will help the Prosecution to produce a list of exhibits and begin disclosure of exhibits for trial pursuant to Rule 66(B). This process also helps the Prosecution to produce its final pre-trial brief, even though I must state that we are quite far from having reached that stage as yet. In addition, in the course of the last Status Conference, the accused provided the Trial Chamber with three books which he alleged will support his defence. Although the Prosecution indicated in Court that they wanted to have copies, which would be provided by the accused at the next Status Conference, my legal staff inform me that they have been informed by the Prosecution that they do not require any further -- any copies of these three books for the time being. So that is the position relating to Rule 77 material, as far as disclosure is concerned. I think that before I move to Rule 68 material, I will stop here for a moment. I will ask you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if you have any remarks to make on disclosure under Rule 66 and under Rule 67, and I will then give the floor to Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour has summarised the situation correctly except for one little detail. The document that we received from the accused was actual 294 pages long, so much more than you indicated. And we have reviewed this document, but -- and now fully understand the nature of the accused's defence and we will focus accordingly. What can be said already that the accused put forward, a lot of speeches and publications and parts of the speeches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Let's not discuss the merits.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to -- both you and Dr. Seselj, this is a Status Conference and we will restrict it to what is basically related to a Status Conference. The merits of the document, be it 80 or 273 pages. I have it here, as I explained, I haven't -- I have started reading it, but I'm still far away from being fully aware of its contents. Will come up for discussion if and when. It may come up for discussion later on, if it is necessary and if it is brought within the agenda of this Trial Chamber in its pre-trial stage. If you have comments to make on that document, please do it formally when you are completely in a position to do that and when I, as a Pre-Trial Judge, am also in a position to follow. At the present moment, I am not in a position to follow because this has been handed to me only a couple of days ago, as I tried to explain. And it requires time for me to go through it. I want to go through it accurately, not missing a single word, and then when the time is ripe to discuss it, if we come to that, then we will discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not intend to go into the merits of this document. I only wanted to indicate that it will take a lot of time translating matters addressed in this document, and you will therefore have to understand that we need some time to really reflect and analyse everything that is brought forward. That is actually -- that is what I wanted to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. And the same applies to me. Yes. Dr. Seselj, do you have anything to state with regard to Rule 66 and Rule 67 disclosure?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very difficult for me to state my views, in view of the fact that this pre-trial Chamber, some eight months ago, made a decision with respect to my request for the transcript from all the Status Conferences, and the Trial Chamber decided to send me videotapes of those conferences. But I have not received them up until the present day, from the last Status Conference, although your service is capable of providing the transcript as soon as a Status Conference is over. And I learnt that when a special judge came from Belgrade to tell me. So I consider this to be yet another way of impeding me in conducting this process. I would have to have had this aide-memoire in the form of tape, and the transcripts from the Status Conferences, the previous judge, Mr. Schomburg, did supply me that on time. Now something has changed in that respect. So why haven't I received the videotape of the last Status Conference when you all know full well that that was necessary to me to be able to prepare for this particular Status Conference. Secondly, let me say that I did receive the material that we're discussing today, and although I was just provided it half an hour before I left the Detention Unit to attend the Status Conference, I nonetheless have succeeded in reading through the documents. It is the decision with respect to the non-disclosure of material provided by the Prosecutor based on Rule 66(A) and Rule 68 and protected measures and also 68, the disclosure of exculpatory material. Now, I have no particular remarks to make with respect to that ruling except to say that I do have a comment with regard to the definition of the defence, the concept of defence. My defence before this Tribunal is conducted by I myself, by myself alone. There can be no standby counsel who will make up my defence team unless I allow him to do that. And secondly, on the 26th of May, 2003, I submitted to the Appeals Chamber an objection to the decision to provide me with a standby counsel, and I have not received an official response from the Appeals Chamber to the present day, and I don't consider a letter from the Senior Legal Officer as a response. Now, if my objection has some formal drawbacks, then it is up to the Trial Chamber to say that it rejects it because of the form it was written in, but I do not accept being appointed a standby counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, you have -- you can keep on rambling and objecting to the appointment of the standby counsel. I can assure you you're not going to dissuade the Trial Chamber to go back from its decision or to go back on its decision. It's not up to you to accept or not accept the standby counsel. He's there. And Mr. Lazarevic would still be here had he not decided to take criminal action against you. I can assure you, he would still be here. And Mr. van der Spoel will remain here, irrespective of whether you like him or not or whether you want him or not. That is the decision of this Trial Chamber, to have a standby counsel, and if you don't like it and you have -- or you think you may have a remedy, you can make use of that remedy, but I am going to stop you as far as that matter is concerned. With regard to the rest, you are right that -- I agree with you, the decision of the 11th February should have been communicated to you before. But as I said, as far as this Trial Chamber is concerned in relation to the Status Conference of today, if you don't agree with that decision, then file an appeal. You have a time limit within which you can file an appeal, and the matter will be determined then by the Appeals Chamber. With regard to Rule 68 disclosure, I'm coming to it now. Regarding Rule 68 material disclosure, I have the following to state: First of all, I suppose you are all aware that Rule 68 has been amended as a result of -- or by the plenary of the Judges of this Tribunal way back in December, and the amendments took effect in the same month, if I remember well, on the 24th of December. In the second -- in its second report on disclosure, the Prosecution discussed - I must say, I'm using the word "discussed" because you did - the recent amendments to Rule 68, and what the Prosecution considers to be the implications as such amendment as regards disclosure of exculpatory material and other disclosures contemplated under the new Rule 68. The Prosecution explains in its report how it understands the Rule. According to the Prosecution, the Prosecution is now obliged to disclose only that material whose exculpatory character it is actually aware of, and it also contends that no open-source material, such as media articles, published books, would be included, as such materials are easily accessible to the accused. The amended Rule, according to the Prosecution, narrows down the definition of exculpatory material by deleting the words: "In any way tends to," language that existed in the old Rule. And then finally, the Prosecution submits that amendments codify the use of the electronic disclosure system which enables or would enable the accused to search the OTP's, Office of the Prosecutor's collections. According to the Prosecution in that respect, or in this respect, Dr. Seselj's refusal to utilise computers may give rise to a problem, but according to the Prosecution cannot hinder the implementation of the second paragraph of Rule 68 as amended. As a result, or in consequence of this interpretation of Rule 68 by the Prosecution in this case, the Prosecution came out with some suggestions, and I want you to follow carefully what I am saying here, because this is of fundamental importance. The Prosecution states that it will continue disclosing exculpatory material that is in its actual knowledge. Then it states that the accused will have access, with the amendments to Rule 68, to new material, in quotes: Through conducting a search through the electronic disclosure system. However, the Prosecution also acknowledges that the system is not yet fully operational for at least another six to eight months. Therefore, the Prosecution offers to continue searching the new material for exculpatory material until the electronic disclosure system is fully operational. And finally, the Prosecution submits and suggests that even when the electronic disclosure system is fully operational, it will not contain a hundred per cent of the Office of the Prosecutor's evidence collection, as it does not contain Rule 70 material, that is, sensitive witness statements, and the Prosecutor undertakes to perform updated electronic searches on exculpatory Rule 70 material and to disclose this material to the accused, in accordance with Rule 68(C). I want to make myself very clear that it is not and it will not be regular for me, as the Pre-Trial Judge, to pronounce myself now on your interpretation of the newly amended Rule 68. You have an obligation, under Rule 68, as it had been amended. Try to make sure that you read that Rule well. And the Trial Chamber will intervene only if your application of Rule 68, when it comes to disclosure, is alleged not to be regular. But I am not here to give you advice on how Rule 68 should be applied by you. You apply Rule 68 material, and if Dr. Seselj has reason to believe that you have not applied it well or in accordance with the law, then I will make a pronouncement as to what Rule 68 means. And I would also suggest that this is not a matter for interpretation. Interpretation comes into play only when the Rule itself is unclear. And I don't think at the present moment that Rule 68 is unclear. I will certainly draw your attention to the second part of Rule 68, paragraph (B), which significantly starts with the words: "Without prejudice to paragraph (A)." In other words, nothing contained in paragraph (B) should diminish from the rights that Dr. Seselj and any other accused has to have exculpatory material disclosed under paragraph (A) of Rule 68. Beyond this, I am not prepared to go for the time being. The other matter, of course, relates to the second part of Rule 68, the problems you envisage and that I suppose you envisage rightly, when it comes -- or when we come to the stage of disclosure in accordance with that paragraph, that is, disclosure in an electronic form of the material to which paragraph (B) of Rule 68 refers. Now, at this point in time, I think it will be premature and completely out of place to discuss whether this will constitute a problem, to what extent it will constitute a problem, and how we could solve it, because you yourself admit that the electronic disclosure system will at least require another six to eight months to be put in place, and that will happen. By the time that happens, we will have had at least one more Status Conference, if not two. So we will deal with that problem as we go along, and I am sure that we will find a practical -- a practical solution to that, but I don't think it's the case of discussing this any further during today's Status Conference, because it will be a sheer waste of time, not knowing exactly what's going to be entailed and what the situation will be like in eight months' time or even later. As far as I am concerned, this closes the discussion from the Chamber's side on Rule 68 material. I will now address you, madam, if you have any remarks to make on Rule 68 material. But please avoid mentioning or raising the matter related to electronic disclosure system or the interpretation or the proper meaning of Rule 68 at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We just have filed our position in writing. There's nothing to add to this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Dr. Seselj, do you have any comments with regard to Rule 68 disclosure? And I will also request you to refrain from referring to disclosure in an electronic form, as required by the new paragraph (B). That will be dealt with at a later stage, if at all. Do you have any remarks with regard to Rule 68 disclosure?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have been refraining for more than half an hour, or you turn off my microphone. But I have to get a copy of amended Rule 68 in order to be in a position to state anything. But I haven't got it yet. I'm in a very difficult situation here, indeed, because the Court is ignoring me. You did not tell me why you did not submit a video-recording to me, and I have the Rules here dated the 20th of March, 2003. Since then, if there have been any amendments, I have not been informed about them. So how can I state my views now? I have to get the amended Rules first, and then perhaps the best thing would be for you to postpone this Status Conference for another three days so that I could state my views, because I have no idea what is written there. I have Rule 68 here, the one that was valid until March 2003, and I have Rule 68 bis. But this paragraph (B), or (C), if the interpreter interpreted this correctly, I have never seen this before. I am not in a position to consult my legal advisors, as I have been prohibited from using the telephone, and for two months now I have had no contact whatsoever with anyone except for the prison guards. I can have a look at it straight away. You see, I react very quickly. Just give me a copy now and I will be able to state my views. But you have to provide me with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, how easy is it to have a copy of the new Rule 68 in the Serbo-Croat language provided to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just I may be of assistance. The Rule is actually within -- the new version of the Rule is actually cited completely in the motion that we filed -- in the report that we filed, and therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- Mr. Seselj is in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not in a position to say anything. If the Prosecution is quoting a Rule, I have to take their word for it. I do not take the word of the Prosecution for anything, especially not in view of a false indictment against me. I am not going to invoke the interpretation of the Prosecution of this Rule. I want to have the Rule itself. I want an official Court document with the amended Rule. Without it, I cannot invoke it in any way. If I trusted the Prosecution, then, ha, where would that lead me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I am not going to entertain any more complaints now on this, because it transpires that although you told me you are not aware, you were not aware even that this Rule had been amended, you had every indication that it had been amended. And you could have asked, since you decided to defend yourself, to be provided with a copy of this newly amended Rule, and you apparently didn't. So I can't help you there. All I can do is to make sure that you are handed a copy of this Rule as soon as possible, but what you say is no justification for me to postpone or adjourn this Status Conference. Second, other matter that you mentioned. I mean, I am going to be very short, concise on this. This video-recording. I am not aware of your request to have a video-recording, and of course, you will have a video-recording of the last Status Conference, and also of this Status Conference, as soon as possible. The other thing I want to say is that you are the first person I have met, Dr. Seselj, who needs to look at himself on the screen to remember what was stated during the Status Conference in order to be able to prepare for the subsequent Status Conference. With that having been said, we move to the next question, and this relates to disclosure of Rule 68 material in particular, because I attach to this problem a lot of importance. And this is the language problem. During the last Status Conference, Dr. Seselj insisted on more than one occasion that every document provided to him must be in his own language, including -- and particularly including Rule 68 material. On that occasion, I had pointed out two things. The first was that the accused has a right to file a proper motion in which the Trial Chamber will decide whether the material needs to be translated in a language that he understands or not. And the OTP was also advised that service of material on the standby counsel, who is not acting in a representative capacity, cannot substitute for service on the accused. Now, this latter statement still stands, and, Mr. van der Spoel, I would like you to take notice of that. And the other thing that I wish to register is that, to my knowledge, the accused has not filed a proper motion relating to this language problem. Then in its second report on disclosure, the Prosecution discussed the problem again and suggested the following solutions: According to the Prosecution, and according to its interpretation of Rule 68, this would mean that all potentially exculpatory material must be translated into B/C/S and -- must be translated into B/C/S, and if this is so, this would create an onerous and unnecessary burden on the Office of the Prosecutor. As a result, they make the following suggestions, namely, to translate the specific text from each document that is exculpatory into the language of the accused and provide these translations and the source to the accused. According to the Prosecution, this system would allow the accused to receive the actual exculpatory material in the Serbian language without overtly taxing the limited resources of the Prosecution. I would like -- if you have any further comments on this, you are welcome to make them, but I wouldn't imagine that you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I address you, Dr. Seselj, on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is definitely of great importance to you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm just waiting for the interpreter to finish. According to these Rules, everything that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Speak slowly, because if you speak at a fast rate, you will create difficulties for the interpreters. So speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But I'm always very anxious, because you have frustrated me with the way you behave. I always think that you're going to switch off my microphone. Everything I raise orally, verbally, at a Status Conference has the legal validity, or rather, legal significance, of a written submission. Secondly, last year I did inform the Court that I request that all Court documents be supplied to me, and that includes the Prosecution, because the Prosecution, in the broader sense of the word, is part of the Court. And I insist that all these documents be provided to me in the Serbian language, that is, the only language I understand. Quite simply I'm not going to receive anything else that you send me. I have properly signed for everything that you sent me in the Serbian language. As for you, your task is to accuse me and to convict me. You can try me in any language. You can do anything. And that is what I take as my point of departure that you can do anything but I know what I do not have to do. I never have to receive a single document in a language I do not understand. And you will have to translate everything into Serbo-Croat ultimately, because it is your duty to provide me with all of that. That is my law, according to all international documents, according to the international covenant on civil rights, and I'm never going to give up on that. I'm not interested in your problems. I already told you, engage another thousand translators and interpreters. I guess you can get the money from people who will willing to finance you. Your problems are your problems. I am not burdening the Prosecution with my technical problems, and the Court should be interested in my technical problems. As for that video cassette, Judge, I have here a ruling of the Trial Chamber that I get video-recordings of each and every Status Conference, and also, once the trial begins, that I get all the trial recordings every day and that I have the exact minutes and seconds shown when things were said. So that if I possibly lodge an appeal, that I can say exactly on which day, at which hour, and at which minute somebody said something. I have a copy of that. You must have a copy of that. If I have the facilities, I'd photocopy it for you in prison and I'd send you a copy. There is no point in accentuating this question of language any more. It is crystal clear. Everything has to be provided to me in a language which is the only one I understand. The other day the Prosecution tried to send me I think 57 documents on computer diskettes. Again, I cannot accept that. I cannot receive that. How can I deal with these diskettes? Everything has to be on paper. Paper is the basic material that courts throughout the world deal with. What is not on paper is considered non-existent. If there is a replacement for paper then it is only in order to have things handled as easily as possible, but then ultimately all of that has to be on paper as well so it could serve its purpose. So finally everything has to be on paper and everything has to be in the Serbian language. If you have other technical problems, let them open me an office. I am my own defence counsel. Let them open me a defence counsel office at the Detention Unit. I'm in a single cell, like all the other detainees. That's no problem in itself. But the problem is that I have nowhere to store these piles of documents that are being served on me. So according to Rule 68, it is your duty to disclose to me in good time, as soon as you get in possession -- in your possession any exculpatory materials. If you do not do that, there are sanctions provided for in Rule 68 bis, unless that Rule has been amended in the meantime as well. Please bear this in mind. This is a serious Court and this process is too. You are referring to its historical importance in the document that was handed to me today, so in this historical process, do not only ask the accused to become familiar with the Rules of a court through the documents of the Prosecution. This is quite a compliment that you're actually paying me. When I came here, when I set out to come here, first Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and foremost, I knew that this would be a historic trial, no doubt. Again, according to Rule 66, all documents have to be provided to me, everything that is related to my trial, and I insist that all of this be provided to me. The Prosecution said that I did not submit a request for that, and I'm submitting it right now. It was not a priority for me then. It is a priority for me now, especially because I've received information that the Prosecution will not be trial ready before 2006. So I want to deal with everything in good time, so I ask that these documents be provided to me so that I would have enough time. So this is another request I have for the Prosecution. That is what I wish to say, Your Honour, about this particular question, that is to say, acting in accordance with Rule 68, and thank you for not having interrupted me this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rule 68 does not require, Dr. Seselj, disclosure in your language. Other Rules do, but Rule 68 doesn't. And in order to be concise on this, I would suggest that you be given a copy of the Trial Chamber II's decision in the Brdjanin case on the application of Rule 68 disclosure and a translation in -- and translation in the language of the accused. Registrar, this is a decision which was handed down by the Brdjanin -- in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did not give you permission to speak as yet. I will when I have finished, Dr. Seselj. And please do try to remember that I am the Judge here and you are the accused, and that this is no special case and it will not be dealt with as a special case. If you consider it as a historic case, you may be eluding yourself or leading yourself in an alley which I call delusion of grandeur but it is like any other case and it will be dealt with like any other case. So please don't get keyed up on it. You will be dealt with like every other accused here and your rights will be the same as they are sanctioned by our Rules, and no more than that. Anyway, I will give you a copy, Madam Registrar, at the end of the sitting of this decision, and you will then have it -- make sure that it is available also in the language of the accused and have it sent to him at the Detention Unit, because it's a decision which is important as far as the disclosure is concerned. With regard to another matter that was raised by Dr. Seselj in his remarks, and that is his refusal of two CDs that were offered to him on the 9th of February, 2004. I am informed that one of these CDs contains the records of public hearings concerning the events in the Ovcara farm in November 1991, and the other CD, the installation software of the search engine Z search [phoen], version 4, which is needed to view these documents. But I am informed that without prejudice to its further rights at a later stage, the Prosecution will print out hard copies of these public hearings concerning the events in the Ovcara farm. Roughly we're talking of a hundred pages or so. And they will be handed to you in paper form. Let me come now to pending motions. There is the motion filed by the Prosecution for non-disclosure of materials provided pursuant to Rule 68(A)(ii) and 68, and for protective measures for witnesses during the pre-trial stage. As I stated earlier on, the Trial Chamber has issued its decision on the 11th of February, granting the request for the issuance of a non-disclosure order. That's in terms of Rule 53(A). And ordering the Prosecution to provide more information to enable the Trial Chamber to determine the request for pre-trial protective measures. Now, it is clear that the first part can only be dealt with outside this Trial Chamber if, and only if, there is an appeal. With regard to the second part, the Trial Chamber will make an assessment, will assess the Prosecution's request for protective measures in more detail when it has received more information as we try to point out in our decision of the 11th February. Do you have any remarks on this latter part?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. This does not really concern you for the time being. It will concern you if we receive further -- further information. You want to say something else. Yes, go ahead, Dr. Seselj, but please try to be short.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that this does have to do with me and concern me. First of all, not a single gesture on my part or a position on my part have I challenged the identity of any protected witness whatsoever, nor have I ever brought into question the confidentiality of evidence that has been deemed confidential. And I shall abide by that to the end and keep to that obligation. The Prosecution has no reason to doubt at all that I could ever disclose the name of a protected witness or any confidential material, and I do not think that there is any reason for the Prosecution, except if it wishes to gain time, which I think is their basic reason, to insist upon that at all. It is not in my own interests to do that. Why would I want to do that? I am quite convinced that here in the courtroom I will win the witnesses, whether they be protected or not. I will win over them. And, Your Honour, it is the same decision. Please take a look at page 3.2. You speak of the historical importance of this case, and not I myself. And I'm just agreeing with you here and supporting your position on that point. I have not come here with delusions of grandeur. But it is your position and your attitude. Perhaps you will help me build up some delusions of grandeur. But it says here the historical importance of this case and I agree with you there. So you attack me even when I agree with you, let alone when I don't agree with you, so I don't think that is proper at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we will await for further information from you on the -- as a basis for the protective measures that you seek and then we will hand down our decision later on. Now, the second matter in respect of pending motions or pending matters is the accused's objection to the indictment which was filed on the 15th of January, 2004, even though it is dated 24th of December, 2003. Now, the Prosecution responded on the 29th of January, 2004. And the translation, I understand, has been filed on the 10th of February, 2004. I want to make sure, first and foremost, that you, Dr. Seselj, have been served with a copy in your language of the Prosecution's response. Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As a consequence, now I can state that the Trial Chamber, and that's the collegial Trial Chamber, not just me, but the other two Judges as well will start its deliberations on this matter, and when we are in a position to hand down our decision, we will hand down our decision. I can state here that there are some very important matters raised in both the accused's objection to the indictment and the Prosecution's response, which require particular attention by this Trial Chamber, and we will give all these matters utmost attention. Are there any other matters that you would like to raise? I will start with the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, Mr. Saxon would like to address you on the pending motion that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which pending motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The pending motion on the form of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, the Prosecution would like to correct an error in the response that it filed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I will have to go to that first. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has noted an error in paragraph 21 to its response to the accused's objection to the indictment. If I could direct your attention to that paragraph. It is on page 10 of the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The second sentence of that paragraph begins with the word: "Accordingly," and reads this way: "Accordingly, the Prosecution has fully and properly pled the jurisdictional prerequisites for crimes against humanity with respect to counts 10 and 12 of the indictment." The word "12" is an error here, Your Honour. That should be "11."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it should read: "And his complaints based on the principle of nullum crimen sine lege in paragraphs 10 to 11 above."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm speaking about the following sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Accordingly, the Prosecution has fully and properly pled the jurisdiction prerequisites for crimes against humanity with respect to counts 10 and 11 of the indictment."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, and we wanted to draw your attention and the attention of the accused to that error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition, the Prosecution has prepared an oral submission regarding the merits of some of the objections made by the accused to the indictment, and with your leave, I will make that submission. It will take five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused argues in his objection to the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me make one thing clear, Mr. Saxon, that I do not expect Dr. Seselj to be prepared to respond to your oral submissions today. This was not expected and not exactly normal. So I will not ask him to respond today. If need be, we will have another Status Conference, in the course of which he will respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honour, the accused argues in his objection to the indictment that this Tribunal cannot have -- cannot exercise its jurisdiction under Article 5 of the Statute over the crimes alleged in counts 10 to 11 of the indictment. These are crimes that were alleged to have occurred around the town of Hrtkovci which is located in the Republic of Serbia. The accused alleges that no armed conflict occurred in the Autonomous Republic of Vojvodina. Therefore, no jurisdiction lies. Your Honour, the standard for this Tribunal's jurisdiction over Article 5 charges was set by the Kunarac appeal judgement, case number IT-96- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, because this is not regular. I don't think that the Status Conference is meant to cover such submissions. If you have further submissions in addition to what you have already filed, please reduce them into writing, have them translated into the language of the accused, and then the accused will have an opportunity to respond further to these additional submissions. But I'm not going to reduce a Status Conference to a debate on pending -- on the contents, on the merits of pending motions. That's not the purpose of a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any further matters that you would like to raise from the Prosecution's side?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Are there further matters that you would like to raise, Dr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have several matters that I have to raise today, because they are of the nature of a Status Conference. And Your Honour, a moment ago you said that I should be provided the ruling in the Brdjanin case with respect to the exculpatory material to be provided in the Serbian language. You know that Mr. Brdjanin has his attorney, and pursuant to the Rules, all attorneys must know either English or French. Now, as I am defending myself, I don't know why I need it, although of course I would like to read it, because I don't myself have to know English. Now, if I have to know the English language, then it's your duty to teach me English. My rights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will interrupt you, because when you try to reduce the proceedings to ridicule, like you are trying to do now, I will stop you. I am the Judge. You are the accused, Dr. Seselj. There are the Rules and you will have to stick by the Rules, and I will apply them and if it needs be to shut you down completely, I will shut you down completely. If you don't want a copy of the judgement in the Brdjanin case, which I kindly offered you, you won't get it. If you don't want it, I won't give it to you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing was ever ridiculous to me here, Your Honour. No ridicule at all. Nor was anything funny to me. I have not laughed throughout this Status Conference, so I don't see why you started today's Status Conference in so much anger. I assume that some reason for that exists, but I don't think that I caused that. I would like to receive that document. I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that it cannot refer to my own case. Secondly, I should like to inform you that there have been violent -- great violations of my rights as the accused and a person in detention. I have been deprived the right of any visits and any contacts at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will stop you here. If you have reasons to complain about the way you are being treated in the detention, you've got remedies. The remedies are not to bring them up in the course of a Status Conference. The remedies are in accordance to the Rules that you have, which regulate the Detention Unit, and in particular, the right that you have to have direct access to the President of this Tribunal, under Rule 19(A) of the Rules. But it is not within my jurisdiction as the Presiding Judge or as a Pre-Trial Judge to tell the commandant of the Detention Unit how to deal with you. So I will only deal with matters. You can mention these matters here in the Status Conference. Just mention, and I will tell you: Yes, you can go ahead, or no, you can't go ahead with discussing this matter here in the Status Conference. You have a right to appeal directly to the President of the Tribunal. So I hope I have made that clear to you. This is not a forum for you to discuss everything that comes to your mind. This is a Status Conference, and we will discuss only matters which are related and pertinent to the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, practice in Court so far speaks otherwise. I would like to remind you that at the last Status Conference you asked me whether I had any comments to make with respect to the conditions of detention and I said that I did not because I did not at the time. Now when you know full well that I do have a lot of objections to make, you wish to avoid that. Therefore, I assume that that Rule might have been changed from the end of October to the present day perhaps, and pursuant to Rule 65 bis(A)(ii) I do enjoy the right to speak on issues which I consider to be linked to the trial and my case, including my health, both physical and mental. And you're now preventing me in doing so, because you know full well that in my particular case, international law has been violated, I have been condemned to death, and had I been condemned to death, my family would not have been allowed to visit me, and that is what has been done here. You don't want to hear about that. If you want to prevent me in saying all this then I won't bring the matter up. But I have the impression, Your Honour, that your nervousness and anger seems to want to provoke some reaction on my part, a turbulent one, and then this to be cause for an incident to arise and for me to be taken out of the courtroom. No, Your Honour. I should like to tell you that nobody can provoke me in that manner because I am in full control of myself. So there's no need for you to show anger. If I'm accused here, I don't show anger towards you or towards the Prosecution so there's no reason for you to demonstrate anger either, unless you're motivated by any personal reasons which I do not know about. So do you still abide by what you said that you're not going to allow me to speak about the conduct of the Registry towards me? I'm not complaining of the Detention Centre but the Tribunal that has unlawfully set itself out as an institution. I have not been disciplined, I'm not being sanctioned, but I am being kept in total isolation because my political party was very strong at the latest elections and the decision to isolate me says that the problem is that we won 82 seats in parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this is not a political platform. I will not allow you to make any political speeches. If you have specific complaints regarding your detention, I ask you mention them and I will immediately tell you this is something that is pertinent to the Status Conference, this is something which is not pertinent to the Status Conference. This is something for which you have a remedy under Rule 19 of the Rules, of the applicable Rules. So let's not waste time. If you have specific complaints, do mention them and we will deal with them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to have this paragraph starting from

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: that basically means also that members of the public are being prohibited from repeating or relaying to others what the accused has just stated with regard to another detainee. Dr. Seselj, you have no right to speak like you did with regard to any other detainee, and I will stop you immediately the moment you try again. Plus, this will not be relayed outside this courtroom. When you try to be -- decide to be honest with this Trial Chamber, this Trial Chamber will treat you better. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You, Your Honour, have several times said here already that I should be honest and act accordingly, act honestly, which would imply that I have not been honest thus far. So quite simply I have to protest about conduct of this kind on your part. I have been continuously honest. I am defending my own rights here to the best of my ability, and also adhering to the Rules and Regulations in conformity with the Statute of the International Tribunal, although I challenge the legality of that Tribunal which is also my right. And you have repeated several times to me here that attorney Lazarevic has brought up criminal action for slander against me as if that is something against me. It just demonstrates the kind of man Lazarevic is, not what I am doing, but you are presenting this that I seem to recognise in this contact some very negative emotions expressed through your own words. So I think you'll be the first to testify in my advantage if Aleksandar Lazarevic brings this criminal action to Court. And I don't think there will be any trial on that and you as a Judge yourself know full well that for what I say here during the proceedings in defence of my rights I cannot be taken to court criminally before another court, especially not a national court, let alone the fact that I only spoke the truth. However, there are some other problems here, Your Honour, so you can interrupt me straight away, and whenever you interrupt me, I accept that quite calmly and don't proceed, because I'm afraid that you'll become even more nervous. On the 20th of October I tabled a request to the Registry that the International Tribunal should take part in the financing of my defence. To the present day, I have received no response from them and my legal advisors are already asking to be paid, and this is an enormous money because they did a lot of work in drawing up the document that numbers 300 pages that the OTP is referring to and the motion with regard to the indictment and whether other potential defence witnesses and their calling [as interpreted]. So I demand that my defence be financed in the extent to which the International Tribunal is duty-bound to do so, bearing in mind the conducts of this Tribunal in all the other cases and that it be applied to my own. Because my legal advisors will no longer wish to work for me if I don't pay them, so what am I going to do then? How can I come to terms with the enormous mechanisms that the OTP has at its disposal. Secondly, I can say with satisfaction that you have already legalised in an indirect way the work of my legal advisors by the fact that the documents compiled by them in my own name and signed you are taking into consideration. So you should draw the attention of the Registrar not to mistreat me in that way and to agree with them so that I can have communication provided for by the Rules that nobody can prevent me in having when they isolated me and brought the decision to isolate me and not to allow me to talk to anybody except my legal advisors and the consul. I asked to talked to my legal advisors and the guards offered me Aleksandar Lazarevic. So they have curtailed that right as well. And I'm bearing in mind a historical legal example. When Adolf Hitler took Georgi Dimitrov to trial under the false indictment to -- for setting fire to the Reichstag, Georgi Dimitrov, in front of Hitler's court, was given the chance to defend himself and to defend himself successfully and no legal principle was overruled with that. I have no chance here. There was always somebody who is angry, who raises his voice, who interrupts me, and with respect to my own rights, this Tribunal is far worse than Hitler's court that took Georgi Dimitrov to trial. So that is my professional opinion as to that question as a legal man myself, Your Honour. Even if there was somebody else sitting here, I would have that same view and hold that same opinion. Why are you afraid of my words? Why are you always redacting things from the transcript? I have experienced here that you, from my written submission that I sent to the Trial Chamber, deleted certain words that I used there. Once it was photocopied, there was white ink written up over it and it was thrown out in the translation. I don't know that there is a single court behaving in that way. And I did not mention a protective witness. I did not bring up any protected piece of evidence or material which would come under the Rules in this respect and could not be accessible to the public. So here it seems that from one case to the next, conduct changes and is not aligned with the law. It is sometimes aligned with personal interests, personal animosity, open hatred at times and so on and so forth. And I really don't know how long this is going to last. And finally, I should like to say the following to you: I am ready to have my case go to trial immediately. I have tried to have legal advisors; you haven't let me have them. I have tried to have the court participate in the payment for my defence. There's no response, which means rejection. So there's nothing left for me to try and do. And I'm ready for the trial to go ahead tomorrow if necessary. I have nobody to table my submissions to. You have isolated me from my family and so that is a fait accompli, as far as I'm concerned, and this is an indication for the public of what kind of Tribunal this is. And I'm not going to write to the President of the Tribunal with my complaints. I will remain isolated rather than have to write a letter to him, and you can draw the conclusions you wish to draw. I am ready, I'm trial ready. We can go to trial tomorrow, and you'll see that the Prosecution won't be ready even by 2006 because they raise the indictment first and then began looking for material to substantiate their case subsequently, and this has brought them into a situation where they don't know what to do with the indictment itself. They had political interest to raise the indictment but they now don't have the legal arguments to substantiate it. So that's what happened in this case. So if that's the case for your dissatisfaction and your terrible anger then I understand you. But I'm not -- that is not something that angers me because I have come here to win and I shall win because I have more forcible arguments than the Prosecution does. And through the force of argument I am going to win. You have supported the head of the Detention Unit not to allow to photocopy a single material for me and I can say that I can have the right to photocopy any material for my defence but my associates won't be able to circulate it if it is confidential, and I have to inform you what -- who those individuals are so that they should not disclose these matters and not be held in contempt of Court. Now, where am I going to photocopy this material? I would have more material to supply the OTP with but I cannot do so because I cannot photocopy any documents. So we can either normalise the situation here to enable a normal trial or that will be it. And let me conclude by saying the following: It is far more to my advantage the hatred you have shown towards me, constant interruption, constant deriding, isolating me from my family and the public, that is far to my advantage. It is a -- rather than if you had an offensive of graciousness sticking to the rules, enabling me to enjoy all my rights perhaps in that way you would be disarming me. However, this way you have strengthened me in my conviction that you're not a proper Tribunal, that you're an unlawful organ -- institution who through a criminally -- criminal act was set up by the Security Council and that that organ is not capable of bringing this process to a close against me because it just doesn't know how to proceed. You're conscious of that, so you haven't written that this is a process of historical significance. You are quite aware of the fact that generations of legal men are learning a lesson of how they should proceed in court cases, using this case as an example. I'm not going to table any more submissions. There's no reason for me to do that. There's no need for me to burden the OTP. If they disclose some materials, well and good. If they don't disclose anything, they haven't got any money to translate them, or whatever, they don't have to do so. Let the trial begin. Let's see what the OTP has at its disposal. And then you'll come to see that the Prosecutors themselves have nothing in their hands, nothing at their disposal, and that is why everything that you've been doing for the past year and everything that's being happening here for the past year is because you're faced with a situation of that kind. Thank you nor not interrupting me this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the part of Dr. Seselj's speech relating to his request to the Registrar to have, according to him, his legal advisors be paid from the funds of the Tribunal be singled out and copied to the Registrar for his attention in case the matter is still pending or needs his attention to it. But for the record, I think the of representation, as far as Dr. Seselj's request to have counsel appointed for him, has been already dealt with at various levels in this Tribunal and there are decisions in accordance to which the Registrar is expected to act. With regard to your state of health, Dr. Seselj, are there any matters or any matter that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at every Status Conference you and your predecessor have been putting this question to me, and then you accuse me of having hidden certain things from you in relation to my health. I never hid anything. The vague statement made by the nurse that there may be an operation next week, that is no appointment. You know full well how appointments of that kind are made. But perhaps I made a mistake for having complained about my health at all. Perhaps it would have been more in line with the kind of court this is for me to remain the way I am, without an operation, and let me go on for as long as I can go on. Secondly, at four Status Conferences - this is the fourth - and at the Initial Appearance, I put the question of mental suffering forth because of the clothing I have to wear, in view of your Rules. Judge Schomburg said that he would provide me with the Rules that governs the clothing that is worn in the courtroom by all involved. I have not received these Rules yet. Last time when I talked about that problem, you laughed, and that is a very serious problem for me. And you have to persuade me that I have to suffer for this, watching you wear this kind of Roman Catholic robes and so on. Because in my court, no such -- in my country, in the courts in my country, no such clothing is worn. Judges and everybody in court wear decent civilian clothes. Please don't misunderstand me. Please take this quite seriously. The Court has to take a position of principle about this. Who established this, on what basis, and for what reasons, and why precisely such attire? That is so frustrating to me. You see, after the Judges and the Prosecutors and the standby lawyer and the Court officials appear in such clothing, I expect to be boiled in a cauldron after that, tortured, killed. That is the kind of thing that comes to my mind, this kind of attire that you wear. It is just like an SS or Gestapo uniform, as far as I'm concerned. The history of my people has identical experience with this kind of clothing worn by the Roman Catholic Inquisition and also the experience we've had with the Gestapo, the SS, et cetera. So once and for all, please take a stand with regard to such matters, and don't say that I am dealing with this frivolously. I'm not. I'm not dealing with any of this frivolously. The Court has to take a position on this and explain why it is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Dr. Seselj. The Court will do nothing about this, what you have mentioned. If it is a problem to you, I am afraid you will have to live with it. And if my predecessor, Judge Schomburg, said that he would provide you with the Rules that govern the clothing, et cetera, I am reversing that decision. I will provide you with nothing. These are our robes, and if you don't like them, look in some other direction. Anything else before we rise? So I declare this Status Conference to come to an end now. The next Status Conference will be convened in accordance with the Rules, that is, within 120 days from today. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: page 32, line 22 -- sorry.  Line 24 to be redacted, to be redacted, and
--- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
